index.note: the peak FM index: how many sidebands the tone carries -- how bright and rich it is. As it rises the spectrum brightens steeply while the loudness stays constant (a balance stage holds the level), so only the colour moves, never the volume.

mellow.gloss: few sidebands, close to a pure sine -- soft and round

bright.gloss: a full, singing brightness with rich sidebands

harsh.gloss: hard and edgy, the sidebands crowding the top

screaming.gloss: the brightest, most aggressive FM -- sidebands to the ceiling

ring.note: how long the bright attack rings before the tone darkens. Every FM note begins bright and loses its highs as it is held -- never its loudness. Low collapses to a dark body almost at once; high stays bright deep into the note.

quick.gloss: the brightness collapses almost at once, leaving a dark body

medium.gloss: the bright attack settles into a darker sustain

long.gloss: stays bright well into the note before it darkens

detune.note: a second voice offset a fixed few Hz above the first, so the two drift against each other and the tone undulates. At 0 it stands perfectly still (the static escape); higher is a wider, more present movement. The offset is fixed in HERTZ, so it is the same at every pitch -- not a cent detune that scales with the note, and not pitch vibrato, which belongs to the synth.

pure.gloss: a single still tone, the two voices locked together

gentle.gloss: a slow gentle drift between the two voices

ting.note: the metallic 'ting' of the attack. this is the single feature that separates an electric piano from a plain fm tone; at 0 the instrument is only its wooden body. the ting fades back into the body as the note is held -- it loses its brightness, never its loudness.

none.gloss: no metal at all, just the woody body

soft.gloss: a faint chime on the attack

clangy.gloss: a hard bright metallic clang on every note

ring.note: how long the metallic part keeps ringing before it settles into the body. short is a quick struck-tine click, long is a sustained metallic buzz that stays through the note. both ends are taken from real electric pianos: the short end is a rhodes-like tine, the long end a wurlitzer-like reed.

short.gloss: a quick click, gone almost at once

long.gloss: a metallic buzz that stays through the note

hollowness.note: the body's character, from full to hollow. low keeps every harmonic and sounds broad and piano-like; high keeps only the odd harmonics, which is what makes a reed sound hollow and nasal. 'tine' is where a classic electric piano sits.

full.gloss: broad and full, every harmonic present

tine.gloss: the classic tine electric piano body

reed.gloss: hollow and nasal, a reed rather than a tine

strike.note: how hard the hammer hits: how bright the body starts before it softens. this shapes the tone, not the volume -- a hard strike is brighter, not louder.

soft.gloss: mellow and round from the first moment

hard.gloss: struck hard, bright and biting before it settles

pitched.note: how definite the pitch is. an ideal stretched membrane rings at spacings that are not whole-number multiples, so it has no clear note -- that is a tom. loading the head with air in a kettle pulls those spacings towards whole numbers until a real pitch appears -- that is a timpani. this is the deepest thing about the instrument, not a tuning offset: the played pitch itself never changes here, only whether the drum sounds like it HAS one.

tom.gloss: no clear note, just a low woody thump

mixed.gloss: a note starts to emerge from the thump

timpani.gloss: a real singing pitch, a tuned kettledrum

strikepos.note: where the head is struck. dead centre wakes only the modes that breathe evenly across the whole skin, which is round and deep; nearer the rim wakes the ones that ripple around it, which is thinner, harder and more sharply coloured. a real player uses this constantly.

tension.note: how tightly the head is stretched, heard as which partials carry the sound rather than as pitch. slack leaves only the lowest ones and sounds dull and floppy; tight brings the upper ones up and sounds bright and taut.

damping.note: how freely the head is allowed to ring, as with a hand or a felt ring on the skin. open leaves narrow clear resonances that sing; muffled broadens them until the drum reads as a thud with a colour rather than a tone.

muffled.gloss: dead and thuddy, a cloth on the skin

index.note: the peak FM index: how many sidebands the tone carries -- how bright and rich it is. As it rises the spectrum brightens steeply while the loudness stays constant (a balance stage holds the level), so only the colour moves, never the volume.

mellow.gloss: few sidebands, close to a pure sine -- soft and round

bright.gloss: a full, singing brightness with rich sidebands

harsh.gloss: hard and edgy, the sidebands crowding the top

screaming.gloss: the brightest, most aggressive FM -- sidebands to the ceiling

ring.note: how long the bright attack rings before the tone darkens. Every FM note begins bright and loses its highs as it is held -- never its loudness. Low collapses to a dark body almost at once; high stays bright deep into the note.

quick.gloss: the brightness collapses almost at once, leaving a dark body

medium.gloss: the bright attack settles into a darker sustain

long.gloss: stays bright well into the note before it darkens

detune.note: a second voice offset a fixed few Hz above the first, so the two drift against each other and the tone undulates. At 0 it stands perfectly still (the static escape); higher is a wider, more present movement. The offset is fixed in HERTZ, so it is the same at every pitch -- not a cent detune that scales with the note, and not pitch vibrato, which belongs to the synth.

pure.gloss: a single still tone, the two voices locked together

gentle.gloss: a slow gentle drift between the two voices

instruments.why: a wire under tension, plucked once and then left alone: the note is made by the pluck and nothing feeds it afterwards, so it rings and dies the way a real wire does -- long and singing at the bottom of the keyboard, a short bright tick at the top. This is NOT `string`, which is a comb resonator fed the whole time so that a held note stands; it is the other thing, an actual travelling wave in a wire, and it is the only entry in the library that fades by itself. Karplus-Strong with the Jaffe-Smith extensions (David A. Jaffe and Julius O. Smith, 'Extensions of the Karplus-Strong Plucked-String Algorithm', Computer Music Journal 7(2), 1983), as Csound's `wgpluck2` implements it: two delay rails with a one-pole reflection filter standing in for the bridge. THREE THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE REACHING FOR IT. (1) IT TAKES THE KEY AT THE START OF THE NOTE AND THEN HOLDS IT. `wgpluck2` reads its frequency at i-rate, so the `reinit` on `ktrig` in the code is what makes it play the note at all -- and glide, pitch bend, vibrato and everything else on the pitch bus do not reach it once the note has begun. A legato slide leaves the wire at the pitch it was plucked at. A note that has to bend needs a pitch-following body beside it via `+`. (2) IT DECAYS, and how fast depends steeply on the pitch. Measured at the oscillator's default 4x oversampling, time to fall 20 dB: at refl 0.70 a note at 110 and 220 Hz has still not dropped 20 dB after 25 seconds, 440 Hz takes 4.4 s and 880 Hz 0.54 s; at refl 0.85 that is 8.5 s at 220, 1.05 s at 440 and 0.14 s at 880. So a long held note in the top octave will have gone silent by itself while the key is still down. That is the wire, not a fault -- but it is why this entry does not answer a prompt that asks for a sustained tone. The ring length also follows the LRO's oversampling setting, and steeply: at 1x that same 440 Hz note is down in 0.18 s where 4x gives 2.3 s. The model grows its delay line by whole periods until it holds at least 512 samples and rescales the reflection to match, so a shorter line -- a lower rate or a higher note -- ends up with a lossier bridge. It cannot be undone from outside: unwinding that rescaling would need a reflection below zero, which the model does not accept. Every figure here is at the default. (3) IT PLAYS SLIGHTLY FLAT, more so the higher the note and the higher refl. The bridge filter's pole is refl itself, so raising it adds delay to the loop, and the loop's length is the pitch; the delay line is also truncated to whole samples, which bites harder the shorter it is. Measured across the axis: within 4 cents at 110 and 220 Hz, within 18 at 440, and up to 44 cents flat at 880. The mechanism is read off the model's own source; the size of it is not derived, it is declared, and that is why the axis stops at 0.85. ABOVE THE AXIS IS COLOUR, NOT A NOTE. refl 0.90 to 0.98 is a different thing altogether: at 0.98 the sound is gone in 0.17 s at 220 Hz and sits 91 cents flat there, 172 cents at 440. What is left is a crackle, a small dry transient. Worth having -- layered under a pitched body with `+`, never asked to carry the pitch. THE PICKUP POINT IS THE SECOND AXIS. `pick` is where along the wire the sound is heard, and it is real geometry: a harmonic whose still point falls on that spot is simply missing. At 220 Hz, read over the first half-second because the note is already dying after that, the second harmonic runs from -7.0 dB below the fundamental at 0.25 to -11.0 at 0.35, and the third drops into a 68 dB hole at 0.33 -- wiry, then reedy, then round. It moves the LEVEL as well, and the body declares that instead of hiding it (`; LOUDNESS: pick`): across the axis the peak falls 1.25 dB while the note's settled energy RISES 1.75, in opposite directions, and the peak moves by the same amount at every register (-1.24 to -1.25 dB from 55 to 1760 Hz). What travels is the distance between them -- the peak sits 9.7 dB above the settled level at 0.25 and 6.7 dB at 0.35 -- because the wave is spiky near the end of the wire and smooth further along. That is a pluck being a transient, not a volume control, and it is the case §4 stopped judging by threshold on 2026-07-27. Both figures are `lco_measure`'s own peak and rms at the oscillator's default 4x. THE AXIS STOPS AT 0.35 FOR MOVEMENT, NOT FOR LOUDNESS. Raising the pickup damps the colour's travel over the note (46 Hz at 0.25, 20 at 0.35, 16 at 0.37), and at 0.37 combined with the shortest ring (refl 0.85) the body stands still outright when the LRO is run at 1x oversampling. 0.35 is the last point that still moves at every refl and every oversampling setting. Beyond it: at 0.50 the colour stands still at 55, 110 and 220 Hz, and past 0.50 nothing is new -- that is the middle of the wire and everything beyond mirrors what came before, 0.80 measuring within 3 dB of 0.20 over the first six partials. The middle itself, 0.50, kills the even harmonics outright (second harmonic 43 dB down at the attack) and stands still: a striking sound, and a deliberate one -- set it by hand, outside the axis. TWO NOTES ON THE CODE. There is deliberately NO `dcblock`: `wgpluck2` produces no DC worth blocking here (0.05 % of rms at worst), while `dcblock2`'s corner scales with the sample rate, so at the oscillator's 4x it becomes an ~800 Hz highpass that takes 23 dB out of a note at 110 Hz -- it destroys exactly the low end this body is good at. And `PLUCKWIRE:` is a LABEL, which cannot be indexed the way this library's variable names are: a second copy of this body in the same instrument must be given a different label. wave.note: which waveform. 0.0 is a triangle, 0.5 a sawtooth, 1.0 a pulse of the width set by `width`. Below 0.5 it is one vco2 rail in imode 4, where the pulse-width argument is the ramp's shape; above 0.5 it crossfades to a second rail in imode 2, where that same argument is the duty. Measured at 220 Hz: the spectral centroid runs 614 Hz at the triangle, 2211 at the saw, 5696 at a square, and the level holds to 0.35 dB across the whole axis -- so this is a colour control, not a volume control.

triangle.gloss: the fewest harmonics of the three

pulse.gloss: the pulse rail; `width` then decides its duty

width.note: the pulse duty -- the ON fraction of one period -- and it only acts once `wave` is in the pulse half. 0.5 is a square (odd harmonics only); away from 0.5 the even harmonics come in and the nth harmonic is cancelled wherever n*duty is a whole number. 0.12 and 0.88 sound alike because a pulse and its complement have the same magnitude spectrum. Two things are handled in the body rather than left to the player: a duty off 0.5 carries a DC offset of A*(2d-1), removed exactly; and the level is held (rms 2A*sqrt(d(1-d)) normalised out), so the measured spread over the whole range is 0.08 dB.

narrow.gloss: thin and nasal; the reedy end

wide.gloss: the mirror of narrow, same spectrum

pwm.note: how far the duty swings, at `rate` per second. 0 leaves the width standing where `width` put it. This is pulse-width MODULATION -- the width in motion -- and it is what makes one oscillator sound like it is breathing. The sweep goes THROUGH the square: as the depth rises the swing recentres on duty 0.5, so at full depth it crosses the square from either side of it and the even harmonics vanish and return once per swing, whatever `width` is set to. Measured at 220 Hz, even-to-odd harmonic energy runs 0.08 to 0.94 at full depth and is the same at width 0.12, 0.30 and 0.50; the sweep stands still only at its two turning points (9 % of the note). Colour travels 731 Hz of centroid while the level travels 0.36 dB.

gentle.gloss: a slow breathing under the tone

full.gloss: the duty crosses the square from both sides, evens in and out once per swing

rate.note: how many times per second the width completes a swing. Slow is the classic string-machine drift; above about 4 the swing itself becomes a timbre rather than a movement. Has no audible effect while `pwm` is 0.

fast.gloss: fast enough to hear as texture

finetune.note: cents off the played note, so two or three layers of this oscillator can be detuned against each other -- the octave knobs the player has (koct1/2/3) move in octaves and cannot do it. Beating between two layers a few cents apart is what makes a sound thick; that thickness is composed from layers here and is not a knob on one oscillator. Measured: -25 asked gives -25 heard.

flat.gloss: a slow beat against a layer at zero

sharp.gloss: the same beat the other way

drive.note: how hard the oscillator is pushed into a soft limiter. `balance` holds the result at the clean signal's level, so this adds harmonics without adding loudness: measured 0.00 dB across the whole axis. On a saw the spectral centroid runs 2177 Hz at 0 to 6234 Hz at 1. What it does depends on the waveform, and the entry says so rather than pretending otherwise: a limiter first ROUNDS a shape and only then clips it, so a triangle -- which has almost no harmonics to begin with -- goes darker before it goes brighter (598 Hz down to 306 at drive 0.2, back up to 798 at 1). A saw shows the same dip but only 91 Hz of it before it climbs.

warm.gloss: clearly harder than clean, not yet fully clipped

age.note: how far the components have drifted: a slow pitch wander, a jitter on the duty, and a slow level wobble, each scaled by this one value and each at its own unrelated rate so they never lock. At 0 the oscillator is mathematically exact and sounds it. Every voice enters the drift at a different phase, so a chord does not wander in lockstep.

instruments.why: air blown across the mouth of a bottle: a wide, soft, almost noteless tone with only two or three partials over the breath, and it stands as long as it is blown. Built from Csound's waveguide clarinet bore with its breath at the documented ceiling, where the reed stops reading as a reed and what is left is air over an opening; the bore's upper colour is then cut back to how open the blow sounds. NOT the reed instrument (`clarinet`) and not a struck vessel. blow = from a dull hoot with barely more than the fundamental, through the two spots that read as a real blown bottle, up to where the tube saturates and nothing further is added.

kdrift  oscili 0.16, 0.07, giSine        ; the blow is never quite steady
kblow   = 0.42 + kdrift
kmult   = 1.2 * (10 ^ kblow)                ; how far up the bore's colour is let through

                                            ; kngain at its documented ceiling (0.5): at the top

instruments.why: a metal body held ringing by moving air rather than struck: three modes at stretched, non-whole-number spacings, driven continuously by filtered noise whose brightness keeps travelling, so the body never settles and a held note stands. Enigmatic rather than like any named instrument -- machine-room, industrial. Same modal filter bank as `struck_bar` and `cymbal`, but a different body: those are tuned bars and cymbals with whole-number-ish or dense spacings, this one is deliberately stretched and its character comes from the drive moving. stretch = from a hollow whole-number tube to a wide stretched bell. drive = how bright the air working the body is.
instruments.code:
kstr    = 0.475                             ; how far the modes are stretched off whole numbers
kr2     = 2.00 + 1.60 * kstr
kr3     = 3.00 + 5.20 * kstr
kdrv    = 0.40                              ; how bright the air driving the body is
kcen    = 600 * (11.667 ^ kdrv)
aexc    rand 0.05
kcut    oscili kcen * 0.35, 0.09, giSine     ; the drive keeps moving, so the body keeps changing
kcut    = kcen + kcut
aexc    butterlp aexc, kcut
a1      mode aexc, kfreq * koct1, 340        ; three modes, driven CONTINUOUSLY rather than struck:
a2      mode aexc, kfreq * koct1 * kr2, 260  ;   a held note stands, and the host owns the note-off
a3      mode aexc, kfreq * koct1 * kr3, 190

bell.gloss: the found body: wide, metallic, no settled note

plate.gloss: far stretched: a plate, all clang and no pitch

drive.note: how bright the air driving the body is, which decides how much of the upper modes ever get woken. measured: centroid 349 -> 526 Hz with the loudness inside 0.2 dB. do NOT reach for the modes' Q instead -- measured over Q 60..1400 that is a 12.3 dB loudness ramp for 56 Hz of colour, i.e. a volume fader wearing a timbre name.

muffled.gloss: worked by dull air; only the lowest mode speaks

room.gloss: the found drive: a machine room

bright.gloss: brighter air, the upper modes come up

hissing.gloss: driven by full-band hiss, all modes lit

motions.why: a glinting in the TOP of the spectrum: the high partials catch the light and let it go again, irregularly. Only the top moves -- the body of the tone stands still. This form re-weights partials that are ALREADY there, so it needs a tone with a bright tail; on a mellow FM tone there is nothing above the highpass to glint with.
